components.note: 宀 (roof) — a peaceful home under a roof relates to 宁's meaning 'calm, serene.'
丁 (dīng) gives a sound distantly related to níng, having drifted apart over time.
心 (heart) — 愿 relates to a heartfelt wish or desire
原 (yuán) gives a loose sound connection to 愿's reading yuàn

example.hanzi: 我宁愿走路,也不想挤公交车。
example.pinyin: Wǒ nìngyuàn zǒulù, yě bù xiǎng jǐ gōngjiāochē.
example.english: I'd rather walk than squeeze onto the bus.
example.fact: 宁愿 typically appears in the paired pattern "宁愿…也不/也不要…" to state a preference between two options ("would rather X than Y") — English "would rather...than" compares directly, while Chinese explicitly negates the rejected option instead.

components.note: 阝 (mound/place) suggests a hidden spot behind a hill.
急 (worried, urgent) suggests someone anxiously ducking out of sight, giving 隐 its meaning 'to hide, conceal.'
目 (eye) — 瞒 relates to concealing something from someone's view.
㒼 (mán) gives the sound — an exact match with 瞒.

example.hanzi: 他一直向父母隐瞒自己辞职的事。
example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí xiàng fùmǔ yǐnmán zìjǐ cízhí de shì.
example.english: He kept hiding the fact that he had quit his job from his parents.
example.fact: 隐瞒 almost always carries a negative charge — the thing hidden (a mistake, a diagnosis, the truth) is something that arguably should have been disclosed — unlike the neutral 保密 ("keep confidential"), which is often entirely proper, as with a trade secret.

components.note: 见 (to see) — the act of looking.
又 (again, or a hand) — looking closely or repeatedly, giving 观 its meaning 'to observe, view.'
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.

example.hanzi: 每个人对这个问题都有不同的观点。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén duì zhège wèntí dōu yǒu bùtóng de guāndiǎn.
example.english: Everyone has a different point of view on this issue.
example.fact: 观 (built from 见 "to see" plus 又, a repeated hand motion) already means "to observe closely," and 点 traces back to a small dot or point of light — together 观点 builds "a point from which one observes," a fairly transparent path to the modern sense "viewpoint, standpoint."

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
木 (wood) — boards and planks like 板 are traditionally made of wood.
反 (fǎn) gives a rhyme close to bǎn, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 请把地板擦干净。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ dìbǎn cā gānjìng.
example.english: Please wipe the floor clean.
example.fact: 板 (from 木 "wood" plus the phonetic 反) means "a board, plank," so 地板 literally pictures a wooden floor laid over open ground; usage has since broadened well past wood alone to cover tile, laminate, and stone floors too, while 地面 stays the more general word for "ground" of any kind.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 悲 relates to a heavy, sorrowful heart.
非 (fēi) gives a sound distantly related to bēi, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,她感到非常悲伤。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, tā gǎndào fēicháng bēishāng.
example.english: Hearing the news, she felt extremely sad.
example.fact: 悲伤 leans literary, common in writing or formal speech about grief and loss; in everyday conversation Mandarin speakers reach far more often for the plainer 难过 to describe the same feeling.

components.note: 小 (small) — a narrow point at the top.
大 (big) — a wider base below, together giving 尖 its meaning 'sharp, pointed.'
口 (mouth) — relates directly to 叫's meaning 'to call out, shout; to be named.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jiào.

example.hanzi: 看到蛇,她尖叫了一声。
example.pinyin: Kàndào shé, tā jiānjiào le yì shēng.
example.english: Seeing the snake, she let out a scream.
example.fact: 尖 ("sharp, pointed" — 小 "small" narrowing to a point above 大 "big" at the base) plus 叫 ("to call out") combine almost like a sound picture: a "sharp cry," about as literal as Chinese compounds get.

components.note: 网 depicts a woven mesh net stretched over a frame — a picture of a fishing or hunting net, giving 网 its meaning 'net, network.'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 这些鞋子我是在网上买的。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē xiézi wǒ shì zài wǎngshàng mǎi de.
example.english: I bought these shoes online.
example.fact: 网 originally meant a woven fishing or hunting net (the character itself is a pictograph of mesh stretched on a frame); 网上 — literally "on the net" — is very likely a loan-translation of English "online," borrowed alongside "network" as computing terms entered Chinese in the 1980s–90s.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.hanzi: 说不定他已经知道这件事了。
example.pinyin: Shuōbudìng tā yǐjīng zhīdào zhè jiàn shì le.
example.english: Maybe he already knows about this.
example.fact: 说不定, built from 说 ("to say") plus 不定 ("not fixed, not certain"), sits at the more hedging, "I really can't be sure" end of Mandarin's maybe-words — a shade less confident than 可能 or 也许 — and it can open a sentence on its own the way "who knows, maybe..." does in English.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'

example.hanzi: 马戏团里的小丑逗得孩子们哈哈大笑。
example.pinyin: Mǎxìtuán lǐ de xiǎochǒu dòu de háizimen hāhā dà xiào.
example.english: The clown in the circus made the children laugh out loud.
example.fact: 丑 has several unrelated senses — the 12th of the zodiac's earthly branches, and separately "ugly" — but the 丑 in 小丑 most likely traces to a third, older sense: one of the standard role-types in traditional Chinese opera, the comic character, from which "clown" generalized.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 她正在读一本很有名的小说。
example.pinyin: Tā zhèngzài dú yì běn hěn yǒumíng de xiǎoshuō.
example.english: She's reading a very famous novel.
example.fact: 小说 literally reads "small talk" or "minor sayings"; in classical usage it originally referred to unofficial anecdotes and gossip beneath the notice of serious history-writing, and only narrowed over centuries to its modern sense, "novel, fiction."

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
齿 (teeth) — 龄 originally estimated a person's or animal's age by counting their teeth.
令 (lìng) gives a sound very close to líng, sharing the initial and rhyme — only the tone differs.

example.hanzi: 请问,可以问一下您的年龄吗?
example.pinyin: Qǐngwèn, kěyǐ wèn yíxià nín de niánlíng ma?
example.english: Excuse me, may I ask your age?
example.fact: 龄's semantic component 齿 ("teeth") points to a real practice, estimating age by the condition of the teeth — still literally how a vet judges a horse's age today — and likely the origin of extending "tooth" to the abstract sense "age" in this character.

components.note: Depicts a person standing with legs crossed — the crossing shape gave 交 its meaning 'to intersect, exchange, hand over.'
扌 (hand) — 换 describes an action done by hand, such as swapping or exchanging.
奂 (huàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 换.

example.hanzi: 我们互相交换了电话号码。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen hùxiāng jiāohuàn le diànhuà hàomǎ.
example.english: We exchanged phone numbers with each other.
example.fact: 交换 wants a concrete, countable thing changing hands — gifts, seats, phone numbers — while its cousin 交流 is reserved for exchanging something intangible, like ideas or feelings; mixing the two up is a common learner slip.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — early tallies and charms were carved on strips of bamboo.
付 (fù) gives a sound close to fú, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这份简历完全符合我们的要求。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn jiǎnlì wánquán fúhé wǒmen de yāoqiú.
example.english: This resume completely meets our requirements.
example.fact: 符 (⺮ "bamboo" plus the phonetic 付) refers to an ancient tally: a bamboo or wood token split in two, with each half's cut edge serving as a signature — the two halves "符合" (fit together) only if they were genuinely a matching pair, the root image behind today's sense "to accord with, to meet a requirement."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拥 describes holding someone in your arms.
用 (yòng) gives a sound distantly related to yōng, having drifted apart over time.
扌 (hand) shows the action is done with the arms.
包 (to wrap) — wrapping your arms around something gives 抱 its meaning 'to hold, to hug.'

example.hanzi: 他们在机场紧紧拥抱在一起。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zài jīchǎng jǐnjǐn yōngbào zài yìqǐ.
example.english: They hugged each other tightly at the airport.
example.fact: 拥 and 抱 already each independently mean roughly "to hold in the arms" — 拥抱 doubles up two near-synonyms into one word, the same word-building strategy behind 喜欢 and 应该 elsewhere in this deck.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.hanzi: 你带把伞吧,万一下雨呢。
example.pinyin: Nǐ dài bǎ sǎn ba, wànyī xiàyǔ ne.
example.english: Take an umbrella, just in case it rains.
example.fact: 万 ("ten thousand") plus 一 ("one") literally gives "one chance in ten thousand" — from that image of vanishingly low odds, 万一 became the word for hedging against an unlikely but undesirable possibility, typically opening a clause the way "in the unlikely event that..." does in English.

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual) — 社 relates to worship and community gatherings.
土 (earth) — ancient communities worshipped a local earth spirit together, giving 社 its meaning 'society' or 'community.'
匸 (an enclosure or boundary) — 区 pictures a defined territory.
乂 (a mark, here representing control or division) — dividing land into bounded territories gave 区 its meaning 'district' or 'area.'

example.hanzi: 我们社区新开了一家超市。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen shèqū xīn kāi le yì jiā chāoshì.
example.english: A new supermarket just opened in our community.
example.fact: 社 originally named the local earth-god a village worshipped together — its oldest sense is closer to "the community that shares a shrine" than to any modern institution; 社区's use for "community" in the sociological sense is comparatively recent, part of a wave of social-science vocabulary that entered Chinese in the 20th century.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 助 relates to helping, lending one's strength
且 (qiě) gives a loose sound connection to 助's reading zhù
王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 她是总经理的私人助理。
example.pinyin: Tā shì zǒngjīnglǐ de sīrén zhùlǐ.
example.english: She is the general manager's personal assistant.
example.fact: 助 (力 "strength" plus the phonetic 且) means "to lend one's strength, to help," and 理 (originally the natural grain running through jade, later "to manage, to put in order") combine fairly transparently into "one who helps manage" — a title, not just a helper.

components.note: 日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.

example.hanzi: 谁发明了电话?
example.pinyin: Shéi fāmíng le diànhuà?
example.english: Who invented the telephone?
example.fact: 发明 always takes something that did not exist before — a device, a technique — which is exactly what separates it from the frequently confused 发现 ("to discover"), which uncovers something that was already there all along.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.hanzi: 我正在跟客户通话,请稍等。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhèngzài gēn kèhù tōnghuà, qǐng shāo děng.
example.english: I'm on a call with a client right now, please hold on.
example.fact: 通 ("to pass through, to connect") plus 话 ("speech") gives "connected speech" — a fittingly literal way to name what a telephone call actually is, decades before "connection" became a tech buzzword in English too.

components.note: Depicts a person standing with legs crossed — the crossing shape gave 交 its meaning 'to intersect, exchange, hand over.'
辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 下班时间,这条路的交通特别拥挤。
example.pinyin: Xiàbān shíjiān, zhè tiáo lù de jiāotōng tèbié yōngjǐ.
example.english: During rush hour, traffic on this road is especially congested.
example.fact: 交 (a person standing with legs crossed, "to intersect") plus 通 ("to pass through") build "crossing-through" — routes crisscrossing and passing each other — about as literal a picture of "traffic" as a two-character compound can offer.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 演 originally described water flowing and spreading out, later extended to 'developing, unfolding'
寅 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to 演's reading yǎn, having drifted apart over time
口 (mouth) — 唱 describes singing, an action made with the mouth.
昌 (chāng) gives a sound close to chàng, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这位歌手将在体育馆演唱。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi gēshǒu jiāng zài tǐyùguǎn yǎnchàng.
example.english: This singer will perform at the stadium.
example.fact: 演唱 specifically implies singing as a performance for an audience — on a stage, at a concert — while bare 唱 covers singing in any context, including humming to yourself in the shower; the distinction survives in 演唱会, the everyday word for "concert."

components.note: 千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'
A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'

example.hanzi: 这是一项重大的决定。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí xiàng zhòngdà de juédìng.
example.english: This is a major decision.
example.fact: 重大 only modifies abstract nouns — events, decisions, discoveries, losses — never physical weight; for something literally heavy, Mandarin just uses 重 by itself, with 大 here contributing "magnitude" rather than "size."

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 组 originally meant 'to weave, arrange,' extended to 'group, to organize.'
且 (qiě) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zǔ.

example.hanzi: 这两种颜色组合在一起很好看。
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng zhǒng yánsè zǔhé zài yìqǐ hěn hǎokàn.
example.english: These two colors look great combined together.
example.fact: 组合 is also the everyday word for a music group or idol group in Mandarin pop culture — a 男团/女团 "combination" of performers — an extension of the literal sense "to combine, combination" from mathematics and chemistry into entertainment.

components.note: An altered form of 囟 (the mind/head) — the seat of thought.
心 (heart) — thinking was pictured as an activity of both mind and heart, giving 思 its meaning 'to think.'
心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 这本书介绍了他的哲学思想。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū jièshào le tā de zhéxué sīxiǎng.
example.english: This book introduces his philosophical thought.
example.fact: 思想 carries real intellectual and even political weight in modern Chinese — it's the word in "毛泽东思想" (Mao Zedong Thought) — sitting well above the everyday 想法 ("idea, opinion") in formality, the way "philosophy" outranks "opinion" in English.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唱 describes singing, an action made with the mouth.
昌 (chāng) gives a sound close to chàng, differing only in tone.
A pictograph of half of a split tree trunk, shown in cross-section (compare 爿, the other half) — the source of 片's meaning 'a thin slice, piece.'

example.hanzi: 这家店专门卖老唱片。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn zhuānmén mài lǎo chàngpiàn.
example.english: This shop specializes in selling old records.
example.fact: 片, a pictograph of a split log's cross-section — literally "a thin slice" — named the physical shellac and vinyl discs 唱片 once referred to; Mandarin has kept the same word for "album" even now that most 唱片 are digital files with no disc at all.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骑 describes riding on horseback.
奇 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 骑.

example.hanzi: 这部电影讲的是中世纪骑士的故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng jiǎng de shì zhōngshìjì qíshì de gùshi.
example.english: This movie tells the story of a medieval knight.
example.fact: 士 originally named a class of ancient Chinese warrior-scholars, the lower rung of the old aristocracy; 骑士 ("mounted 士") was coined by prefixing 骑 ("to ride") to translate the unrelated European idea of chivalric knighthood — the same word Chinese sportswriters also use for the NBA's Cleveland Cavaliers.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洗 describes cleaning something with water.
先 (xiān) shares the initial x- with xǐ, though the rhyme has drifted.
手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.hanzi: 洗手间在走廊的尽头。
example.pinyin: Xǐshǒujiān zài zǒuláng de jìntóu.
example.english: The restroom is at the end of the hallway.
example.fact: 洗手间 literally means "hand-washing room" — a polite indirection for the toilet, functionally identical to English "restroom" or "washroom." The blunter, more clinical 厕所 names the same room but sits lower on the politeness scale.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 哈 is the sound made by the mouth while laughing
合 (hé) gives a sound related to 哈's reading hā, from an older, closer pronunciation link
口 (mouth) — 哈 is the sound made by the mouth while laughing
合 (hé) gives a sound related to 哈's reading hā, from an older, closer pronunciation link

example.hanzi: “哈哈,你说得太对了!”他笑着说。
example.pinyin: “Hāhā, nǐ shuō de tài duì le!” tā xiàozhe shuō.
example.english: "Ha ha, you're so right!" he said, laughing.
example.fact: 哈哈 doubling or tripling in Chinese texting and chat (哈哈, 哈哈哈, 哈哈哈哈…) reads as genuinely warm, amused laughter, with more repetitions signaling more amusement — unlike English "ha ha," which can carry a flat or sarcastic edge depending on context.

meanings: (Internet slang) previous poster in a forum thread

components.note: 木 (wood) — buildings were traditionally framed with wood.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 楼.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 楼上住着一对老夫妻。
example.pinyin: Lóushàng zhùzhe yí duì lǎo fūqī.
example.english: An elderly couple lives upstairs.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense, forum culture reused 楼上 for "the poster right before me" — each reply in a thread is imagined as a floor (楼) stacked on the ones before it, so the previous post is, quite literally, "upstairs."

components.note: 圣 is the simplified form of 聖, which combined an ear (耳, listening) and a mouth (口, speaking) above a standing figure — the image of someone who listens and speaks with special insight, giving 圣 its meaning 'holy, sacred.'
讠 (speech) — 诞 originally described boastful, exaggerated speech.
延 (yán) gives a sound distantly related to dàn, having drifted apart over time.
耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 孩子们都相信圣诞老人会送礼物。
example.pinyin: Háizimen dōu xiāngxìn Shèngdàn Lǎorén huì sòng lǐwù.
example.english: Children all believe that Santa Claus will bring presents.
example.fact: 圣诞 literally means "holy birth" — Chinese's calque for "Christmas" as the nativity — and 老人 simply means "old person"; together 圣诞老人, "the holy-birth old man," is a transparent compound built to name a Western figure with no indigenous equivalent in Chinese folklore.

meanings: to be aimed at or against

components.note: 钅 (metal) shows what the object is made of.
十 pictures a thin, straight pin, giving 针 its meaning 'needle.'
又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 这个广告是针对年轻人设计的。
example.pinyin: Zhège guǎnggào shì zhēnduì niánqīngrén shèjì de.
example.english: This advertisement is designed targeting young people.
example.fact: 针 ("needle," a fine point of metal) plus 对 ("facing, directed at") builds a fairly vivid image — "needle-pointed at" — for 针对's sense of being specifically aimed or directed at a particular target, whether a demographic, a problem, or a criticism.

meanings: one point (in a score or grade)
one fen (Chinese currency, 1/100 of a yuan)

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'

example.hanzi: 他们的比赛只差一分。
example.pinyin: Tāmen de bǐsài zhǐ chà yì fēn.
example.english: Their game was decided by just one point.
example.fact: 分 alone already covers a small, fixed unit in several unrelated systems — a minute of time, a point of score, a fēn of currency (1/100 yuan) — so 一分 ("one 分") inherits whichever sense the surrounding context calls for, much like English "a point" shifts between sports, punctuation, and geometry.

components.note: 八 (two hands) — holding something up.
目 (a container/tray) — held between the two hands, the image behind 具's meaning 'tool, utensil.'

example.hanzi: 请给我一个具体的例子。
example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yí gè jùtǐ de lìzi.
example.english: Please give me a specific example.
example.fact: 具 (two hands, 八, holding up a tray, 目) already means "utensil, tool" — something with physical form you can hold — and 体 means "body, form"; together 具体 literally builds "having bodily form," the natural opposite of 抽象 ("abstract").

components.note: 页 (head) — relates to 领's meaning 'neck, collar; to lead,' the head/neck area.
令 (lìng) gives a sound hint — 领 is pronounced lǐng, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.
寸 (a hand) — guiding the way.
巳 (a place) — the destination being pointed toward, giving 导 its meaning 'to lead, guide, direct.'

example.hanzi: 他是我们公司的领导。
example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen gōngsī de lǐngdǎo.
example.english: He is the leader of our company.
example.fact: In Chinese workplaces, 领导 doubles as a direct form of address — employees often call their boss 领导 to their face, the way one might say "boss" in English, rather than using a personal name or a specific title.

components.note: 八 (a hand shape) — one of two hands shown reaching toward the same object.
廾 (two hands together) — jointly holding up one object, giving 共 its meaning 'together, joint, common.'
凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'

example.hanzi: 大家要共同努力才能完成任务。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā yào gòngtóng nǔlì cái néng wánchéng rènwu.
example.english: Everyone needs to work together to complete the task.
example.fact: 共同 is almost always an adverb sitting right before a verb (共同努力, 共同决定, "work/decide together") rather than a free-standing word the way 一起 can be — you'd say 我们一起去, but 共同 needs a verb of shared effort to modify.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 洗 describes cleaning something with water.
先 (xiān) shares the initial x- with xǐ, though the rhyme has drifted.
氵 (water) — 澡 describes washing the body with water.
喿 (zào) gives a sound close to zǎo, the same syllable with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上洗澡。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang xǐzǎo.
example.english: I take a shower every morning.
example.fact: 洗澡 is a "verb + built-in object" compound — 澡 isn't a free-standing noun outside this word — so it can never take another direct object the way plain 洗 does in 洗衣服 ("wash clothes") or 洗碗 ("wash dishes"); "bathe" is baked into the verb itself.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稍 relates to a small amount of grain.
肖 (to resemble) — grain 禾 that only resembles a full harvest, a slightly smaller amount, gave 稍 its meaning 'slightly, a little.'

example.hanzi: 今天的天气比昨天稍微冷一点。
example.pinyin: Jīntiān de tiānqì bǐ zuótiān shāowēi lěng yìdiǎn.
example.english: Today's weather is slightly colder than yesterday.
example.fact: 稍微 rarely modifies a bare adjective by itself — it almost always teams up with a following 一点/一些/一下 (稍微冷一点, "slightly colder") to soften the degree, a pairing that trips up learners who drop the second half and leave the sentence feeling unfinished.

components.note: 饣 (food) shows 饮 relates to consuming something.
欠 (qiàn) gives a sound distantly related to yǐn, having drifted apart over time.
米 (rice) — the grain being measured.
斗 (a measuring ladle) — measuring out rice gave 料 its meaning 'material, to estimate, to reckon.'

example.hanzi: 你想喝点什么饮料?
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē diǎn shénme yǐnliào?
example.english: What would you like to drink?
example.fact: 饮 (饣 "food," narrowed here to drinking, plus the phonetic 欠) means "to drink," and 料, which elsewhere means "material, ingredient" (from an old image of measuring grain with a ladle, 斗), together give the literal "drinking material" — Mandarin's everyday word for "beverage."

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
足 (foot) — relates to 路's meaning 'road, path,' something walked on with feet.
各 (gè) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lù.

example.hanzi: 这条公路直接通向山顶。
example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo gōnglù zhíjiē tōngxiàng shāndǐng.
example.english: This highway leads directly to the mountaintop.
example.fact: 公 (八 "to divide" plus 厶, an old graph for "private") pictures private property being divided up to be shared fairly — the root of "public" — so 公路, "public road," names infrastructure by contrast with any privately owned lane or path.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
页 (head/page) — 题 relates to the forehead or the topmost part, extending to the 'title' or 'topic' placed at the top.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 题 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 这次会议的主题是环境保护。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì huìyì de zhǔtí shì huánjìng bǎohù.
example.english: The theme of this meeting is environmental protection.
example.fact: 主 (originally a lamp's flame and stand, 丶 over 王, "the one who tends the light") narrowed to "main, master," and 题 (页 "head, forehead" plus the phonetic 是) named whatever sits at the top of a document — together, 主题 is close to literally "the main heading."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 海 relates to bodies of water, specifically the sea.
每 (měi) gives a hint of the sound — 海 is pronounced hǎi, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 这片海域曾经有海盗出没。
example.pinyin: Zhè piàn hǎiyù céngjīng yǒu hǎidào chūmò.
example.english: Pirates used to roam this stretch of sea.
example.fact: 盗 by itself means "to steal, a thief," and the same character resurfaces in 盗版 ("pirated edition") for bootlegged books, software, or films — Chinese independently extended "piracy" from sea-robbery to intellectual-property theft, the same metaphorical leap English made with the word "piracy."

meanings: erhua variant of 一點|一点[yi1 dian3]

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: 麻烦你把音乐声音调小一点儿。
example.pinyin: Máfan nǐ bǎ yīnyuè shēngyīn tiáo xiǎo yìdiǎnr.
example.english: Could you please turn the music volume down a little?
example.fact: The 儿 in 一点儿 is erhua — a colloquial retroflex coloring of the final syllable rather than a separate spoken syllable, so despite being written with its own character, 一点儿 is pronounced as a single merged sound, yìdiǎnr, closer to Beijing-flavored speech than the equally correct, un-suffixed 一点.

components.note: The upper part, related to 土, traditionally depicted one person's fate.
干 depicted a contrasting fate — the character set two outcomes side by side, with the fortunate one giving 幸 its meaning 'lucky, fortunate.'
子 (child/seed) — 存's meaning 'to exist, survive' has been linked to a seed persisting to grow.
才 (cái) gives a sound hint — 存 is pronounced cún, sharing the initial consonant though the vowel and tone differ.

example.hanzi: 这次事故只有三名幸存者。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì shìgù zhǐyǒu sān míng xìngcúnzhě.
example.english: There were only three survivors of this accident.
example.fact: 者 is one of Mandarin's most productive suffixes for "the one who does X," turning a verb phrase into a role — 记者 ("journalist," 记 "to record"), 作者 ("author," 作 "to make") — so 幸存者, built on 幸存 ("to luckily survive"), literally reads "one who luckily survived."

components.note: 土 (earth) — relates to 增's meaning 'to increase, add,' piling up earth to increase height.
曾 (céng) gives a sound hint — 增 is pronounced zēng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'

example.hanzi: 今年公司的员工人数增加了很多。
example.pinyin: Jīnnián gōngsī de yuángōng rénshù zēngjiā le hěn duō.
example.english: The company's staff numbers increased a lot this year.
example.fact: 增加 pairs naturally with countable, discrete quantities — 人数增加 ("the headcount increased"), 收入增加 ("income increased") — while its cousin 增长 leans toward rates and trends, as in 经济增长 ("economic growth"); swapping the two is a common slip when learners write about statistics.

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 在所有的学生当中,她的成绩最好。
example.pinyin: Zài suǒyǒu de xuésheng dāngzhōng, tā de chéngjì zuì hǎo.
example.english: Among all the students, she has the best grades.
example.fact: 当中 attaches after a noun phrase in the frame "在...当中" ("among/in the midst of...") much like a postposition — a more formal, literary-leaning alternative to the plainer 中 or 之中 in the same slot.

components.note: An open mouth shape.
Rows of teeth inside the mouth.

example.hanzi: 医生检查了我的牙齿。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchá le wǒ de yáchǐ.
example.english: The doctor examined my teeth.
example.fact: 齿, whose own shape pictures an open mouth (凵) with rows of teeth inside, is the more literary, classical word for "tooth"; 牙 is the everyday colloquial one (牙医 "dentist," 牙刷 "toothbrush") — 牙齿 pairs a classical-register word with a colloquial one into a single neutral, standard term.

components.note: 大 (big) — in 头's simplified form, this element is linked to the idea of 'high' or topmost, since the head sits at the top of the body.
⺼ (flesh/body) — 脑 refers to the brain, a part of the body

example.hanzi: 他做生意很有头脑。
example.pinyin: Tā zuò shēngyi hěn yǒu tóunǎo.
example.english: He has a real head for business.
example.fact: 头脑 usually names mental capacity or wits — 有头脑 ("sharp, clever") — rather than the literal anatomical organ, which Mandarin more often calls 大脑 in a medical context; it's closer to English "brains" in "she's got brains" than to the physical brain itself.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 她被任命为部门主任。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi rènmìng wéi bùmén zhǔrèn.
example.english: She was appointed director of the department.
example.fact: 主 ("main, master") plus 任 (亻"person" plus the phonetic 壬, "to bear a duty") builds "the one who bears the main responsibility" — 主任 is an extremely common title across Chinese schools, hospitals, and government offices, roughly matching English "director" or "head."

meanings: variant of 直升機|直升机[zhi2 sheng1 ji1]

components.note: 十 (here a straight vertical line) — 直 pictures something drawn perfectly straight.
目 (eye) — looking directly and steadily with the eye gave 直 its meaning 'straight' or 'direct.'
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 一架直升机在城市上空飞行。
example.pinyin: Yí jià zhíshēngjī zài chéngshì shàngkōng fēixíng.
example.english: A helicopter is flying over the city.
example.fact: 直升机 literally reads "straight-rising machine," describing exactly what makes it different from 飞机 ("flying machine," any airplane): a helicopter takes off straight up, needing no runway.

components.note: 氵 (water) — thirst is a need for water.
曷 (hé) gives a sound close in rhyme to kě, though the initial consonant has drifted.
Depicts a person standing tall, gazing up at the moon 月 — the image of looking into the distance, the source of 望's meaning 'to gaze, hope, expect.'

example.hanzi: 他渴望能出国留学。
example.pinyin: Tā kěwàng néng chūguó liúxué.
example.english: He longs to study abroad.
example.fact: 渴 ("thirst," built on the water radical 氵) plus 望 ("to gaze into the distance, to hope") combine physical thirst with a long stare toward the horizon — a vivid metaphor for craving, paralleling English's own "to thirst for" knowledge or freedom.
